comprehension.myAnswer: A Strand is an individual evidence bundle containing three things: (1) one constant-size Groth16 proof (three elliptic-curve group elements checked via a pairing product equation), (2) the public claim (statement) it proves—carried inside the proof's two public inputs as a BLAKE2b digest of the statement bytes—and (3) context metadata tying that claim to a specific transaction transition (in the V2 source reading: circuit constants tag, family, predicate_digest, shape_digest, and body_len, plus free booleanized witness bits at bytes 112..339 covering vk_digest through intents_digest, including claimant_vkh, the spent state outref and sequence number, the settlement script, and the catalogue of permitted claims and verification keys). A Web is the complete collection of Strands required by a financial contract to authorize a single transaction step. The contract specifies the required conditions (using reusable claim specifications), and settlement is all-or-nothing: a Web can only authorize a transition when every required condition has coverage from a matching Strand, though a single whole-execution proof can cover multiple conditions.
comprehension.pageEvidence: Section 01 ('What are Webs and Strands?' defines Strand, Web, and claim specification); Section 02 ('How the proof connects to the transaction'); Section 03 ('Step 2: A prover builds the Web' lists spent state, sequence number, settlement script, catalogue, verification keys, signed intents, and claimant); Section 05 ('The statement', 'Proof and verification key'); Section 08 ('What a verifying proof shows' and 'What ties a Strand to its step' specify the two public inputs, BLAKE2b statement digest, circuit constants tag/family/predicate_digest/shape_digest/body_len, and witness context bytes 112..339 from vk_digest through intents_digest).
comprehension.task: (1) What a Web and Strand contain
comprehension.whatIStillCannotExplain: The page never shows the concrete byte layout or schema of a Strand (for instance, what occupies bytes 0..111 before vk_digest at byte 112, or how the statement digest is split across the two public field elements). More fundamentally, it leaves the packaging relationship between a multi-condition proof and a Web ambiguous: when a single whole-execution proof covers all three invoice conditions, does the Web contain one Strand object with three role flags, or three Strand objects sharing the same proof? Finally, Section 08 notes that how the consumer derives and enforces the required set of conditions is still PROPOSED and unimplemented.

comprehension.myAnswer: The Groth16 proof itself does not read the Cardano ledger or verify that its numbers match real inputs or outputs. In the V2 source reading, the transaction-binding fields (vk_digest through intents_digest at bytes 112..339) are free booleanized witness bits that the circuit hashes into the statement digest via an in-circuit BLAKE2b gadget without interpreting them. The actual connection to real transaction inputs and outputs happens on-chain at Layer 7 in the consuming (settlement) validator. When the settlement transaction spends the contract's thread state UTxO alongside the pre-verified proof-claim outputs, the settlement validator reads the real ledger inputs (spent thread datum, outref, sequence number, catalogue/reference data) and real ledger outputs (seller payment, fee output, and continuing thread state datum with updated custody and duties), independently reconstructs the statement bytes and their BLAKE2b digest, and verifies that this rebuilt digest matches the statement digest certified inside each consumed proof-claim output. The validator also directly enforces the owner's signed intent caps (per-asset gross_cap, fee_cap, net_floor, liability_cap, validity window, and nonce = seq) and output allocation rules (either strict one-output-per-obligation or a consumer-recomputed partition for coalesced payments) so one output cannot double-count toward two obligations.
comprehension.pageEvidence: Section 02 ('How the proof connects to the transaction'); Section 04 ('Check the owner’s actual outcome'); Section 05 ('Public information: The statement'); Section 06 ('07 / Verification' and 'How these concerns affect one another'); Section 08 ('What ties a Strand to its step' and 'Effects, allocation and authority').
comprehension.task: (2) How a proof connects to real transaction inputs/outputs
comprehension.whatIStillCannotExplain: I cannot explain the exact deterministic statement-byte layout that both the off-chain Rust BLAKE2b gadget and the on-chain Aiken settlement validator reconstruct from a Cardano ScriptContext/TxInfo, nor how the validator disambiguates which output belongs to the seller versus the fee recipient or change when multiple outputs hold the same asset. I also cannot explain how external facts (DEX oracle prices, variable loan rates, or delivery records) are authenticated on-chain, since Section 08 notes that reference-input reads are only PROPOSED and that a Cardano validity interval neither dates nor authenticates a reference datum.

comprehension.myAnswer: In the page's flagship partial invoice payment example (using the 112 CASH fee-included funding mode): (0) Opening state: An escrow UTxO holds 112 CASH against an opening invoice duty of 100 CASH and a separate reserve obligation of 10 CASH, with a rule that each partial payment costs a 2 CASH program fee (whereas the underlying S12 source open(90,10) funds only 110 CASH and charges the buyer a 3 CASH opening fee). (1) Owner signs limits: Before proving, the account owner signs an off-chain intent setting per-asset caps (gross_cap, fee_cap, net_floor, liability_cap), a validity window, nonce = seq, and the target predicate, VK, and shape digests. (2) Prover builds the Web: Off-chain, the prover runs partial(35) over the private witness and generates Groth16 proof coverage for the three required conditions: Payment calculation (100 CASH duty, 35 CASH seller payment, 37 CASH gross escrow debit), Separate program fee (2 CASH to fee recipient without reducing invoice duty), and Remaining obligations (100 - 35 = 65 CASH unpaid invoice + 10 CASH reserve = 75 CASH total owed, backed by 112 - 37 = 75 CASH left in escrow). (3) Proof claims go on-chain: For each Strand, an Issue transaction submits the Groth16 proof to the C2 claim minting policy, which runs the pairing check and mints a proof-claim output holding minimum ADA and a claim token tied to a claimant and expiry. No CASH moves during Issue. (4) Settlement and readback: A settlement transaction consumes the escrow state UTxO and all required proof-claim outputs (burning their claim tokens) with the claimants' signatures. The settlement validator rebuilds the statements from the transaction, checks the owner's signed intent caps, and enforces that 35 CASH goes to the seller, 2 CASH goes to the fee recipient, and 75 CASH continues in the next escrow state with 65 CASH invoice duty and 10 CASH reserve duty. Finally, the application checks block inclusion and required finality and reads back the actual outputs and continuing obligations against the signed intent.
comprehension.pageEvidence: Section 01 ('Paying part of an invoice' worksheet values); Section 02 ('Invoice payment' inspector states 1, 2, and 3); Section 03 ('How a Web reaches settlement', Steps 1–4); Section 07 ('How do I know the payment happened?'); Section 08 ('Duties, backing and fees', 'Transaction signers and authorization boundaries', and 'Invoice source, asset and funding comparison').
comprehension.whatIStillCannotExplain: First, who signs and pays the ADA fees and min-ADA deposits for the Step 3 Issue transactions? Section 08 explicitly admits 'the supplied material does not state who must sign an Issue transaction.' Second, in an escrow workflow where funds are already locked in escrow, which party (buyer, seller, or both) is the 'owner' signing the Step 1 intent? Third, how does the invoice lifecycle ever finish and close? Section 08 reveals that under the S12 source (110 CASH funding), partial(35) leaves 73 CASH against 75 CASH of duties (2 short), a second partial payment has no extra 2 CASH fee funding action, and even after finish() pays off the remaining invoice balance, S12 has no action to discharge or return the 10 CASH reserve obligation—which permanently blocks V2 Close because a thread with nonzero duty cannot close.

comprehension.myAnswer: A condition is a domain-level contract requirement or rule that a state transition must satisfy (such as 'Payment calculation', 'Separate program fee', or 'Remaining obligations' in the invoice app). A proof is the off-chain cryptographic artifact (a Groth16 proof of three group elements) produced by the prover showing knowledge of a private witness that satisfies a compiled R1CS circuit for a public statement digest; importantly, conditions and proofs are not 1-to-1 because one whole-execution proof can cover multiple conditions at once. An on-chain claim output (or proof-claim envelope) is a Cardano UTxO minted by the C2 claim policy during an Issue transaction after verifying one Groth16 proof. It locks minimum ADA alongside a claim token (distinct from any application asset token), records the verified statement digest, claimant key hash, and expiry on-chain, and executes no financial transfer itself; it serves as pre-verified on-chain evidence that sits locked until a later settlement transaction consumes it, verifies the claimant's signature, matches its digest against the rebuilt transaction statement, and burns the claim token (or until the claimant signs a reclaim transaction after expiry).
comprehension.pageEvidence: Section 02 ('Web PROOF COLLECTION' caption and 'How the proof connects to the transaction'); Section 03 (Steps 2, 3, and 4); Section 07 ('Does a proof claim mint my application’s token?', 'What if the Web never settles?', 'Does splitting a Web into more Strands reduce the cost?'); Section 08 ('Where proofs are checked: the issuance route' and 'Complete and incomplete Webs').
comprehension.task: (4) The distinction between conditions, proofs and on-chain claim outputs
comprehension.whatIStillCannotExplain: When a single whole-execution proof covers all three conditions of an application (as Section 02 and Section 08 say it can), how many Strands and how many on-chain claim outputs are minted on the ledger—one Issue transaction minting one claim output that satisfies all three conditions at settlement, or three separate Issue transactions? The page says 'A Strand contains a Groth16 proof... One proof can cover several conditions' (Section 02) and 'n required Strands mean n Issue transactions' (Section 08), but visually depicts three separate lines entering the Web circle and never clarifies whether 3 conditions covered by 1 proof means 1 Strand/1 Claim Output or 3. Also, why does C2 Issue not check that the claimant matches the statement at issuance (allowing mismatched envelopes to be minted on-chain that later fail at settlement)?

comprehension.myAnswer: Groth16 requires a trusted setup that uses secret randomness ('toxic waste') to generate a public proving key and a public verification key. The setup is divided into two stages: Phase 1 ('powers of tau') prepares universal parameters for a specific elliptic curve, format, and circuit capacity that can be shared across many circuits; Phase 2 derives the circuit-specific proving and verification keys for one exact compiled circuit (fixed R1CS constraint matrices, public-input layout, and bounds). A setup stage is trustworthy only if its transcript verifies and at least one participant destroys their secret randomness (whereas Moriarty's current class-0 test setup is single-party and forgeable by its operator). You count setups by distinct compiled circuits (R1CS matrices), not by logical predicates, application conditions, catalogue claim types, or the seven architectural layers. For N distinct compiled circuits that use a compatible curve and format and fit within one Phase 1 capacity, the required stage count is 1 shared Phase 1 + N Phase 2 stages (for example, 1 shared Phase 1 + 5 Phase 2 stages for 5 circuits). Changing transaction amounts, users, or public inputs reuses existing keys, and a bounded parameterized circuit can cover multiple claim types in a catalogue without new setups; however, changing any constraint, bound, public-input layout, or adding a Groth16 wrapper circuit requires a new Phase 2 setup. Because the current Rust compiler bakes predicate_digest in as a circuit constant, every distinct relation identity currently compiles to a distinct circuit, and no Cardano-wide total exists without a frozen circuit inventory.
comprehension.pageEvidence: Section 05 ('Why there is a trusted setup', 'Phase 1', 'Phase 2', 'Try a circuit count', 'When can the same keys be used again?', 'How many setups for all of Cardano?') and setup-counter.png; Section 06 ('01 / Setup'); Section 08 ('Setup and keys').
comprehension.task: (5) What gets set up and how to count setups
comprehension.whatIStillCannotExplain: Section 05 states that 'A parameterized circuit can cover many claims within fixed bounds. That is how a catalogue can contain more claim types than circuits,' whereas Section 08 ('Setup and keys') states that 'In the current Rust source the predicate digest is a circuit constant, so each distinct relation identity is a distinct circuit.' Because of that tension, I still cannot explain how many compiled circuits (and Phase 2 setups) the page's own invoice example—or the five showcased applications—actually requires: is the 3-condition invoice example 1 compiled circuit (1 Phase 2) or 3 compiled circuits (3 Phase 2s)?

proseProblems.location: Section 02 (Applications -> Web PROOF COLLECTION caption & How the proof connects to the transaction)
proseProblems.problem: Stating that one proof can cover more than one condition directly beneath a diagram drawing three separate lines from three conditions into the Web circle—while Section 01/03 says each Strand carries one Groth16 proof and each Issue transaction verifies one proof—leaves the reader unable to tell whether covering three conditions with one execution proof yields one Strand (and one on-chain claim output) or three.
proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: Each button is a condition the contract requires. One whole-execution Strand—carrying a single Groth16 proof and minting one on-chain claim output—can satisfy all three conditions together, or an application can split them into separate Strands when different parties prove each check.

proseProblems.exactQuote: An Issue transaction verifies one Groth16 proof and creates a claim output holding minimum ADA. This output records checked evidence for later settlement. It does not pay the seller or mint the application’s asset.
proseProblems.location: Section 03 (On Cardano -> Step 3: Proof claims go on-chain)
proseProblems.problem: Steps 1 and 4 name the signing actors ('the owner signs an intent', 'requires the claimants’ signatures'), but Step 3 makes 'An Issue transaction' the grammatical subject, hiding who submits, signs, and funds the minimum ADA for the Issue transaction and how the claimant key hash is attached.
proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: A prover or submitter funds and submits an Issue transaction that verifies one Groth16 proof under the claim minting policy and locks minimum ADA in an on-chain claim output naming the claimant. This output records checked evidence for later settlement without paying the seller or minting the application’s asset.

proseProblems.exactQuote: A parameterized circuit can cover many claims within fixed bounds. That is how a catalogue can contain more claim types than circuits. It does not make the circuit unbounded.
proseProblems.location: Section 05 (The proof system -> One bounded circuit covers several kinds of claim)
proseProblems.problem: This passage implies that a catalogue shares one parameterized circuit across multiple claim types, which clashes unexplainedly with Section 08 ('In the current Rust source the predicate digest is a circuit constant, so each distinct relation identity is a distinct circuit') and never tells the reader how many circuits the page's own invoice example uses.
proseProblems.suggestedRewrite: A parameterized circuit can cover multiple claim types within fixed bounds so a catalogue needs fewer circuits than claim types. When a compiler instead fixes each predicate digest as a circuit constant (as in the current Rust prototype), each distinct relation compiles to its own circuit and needs its own Phase 2 setup—for example, one whole-execution circuit for the partial-invoice action versus separate circuits per condition.

summary: As a mobile-first technical reader judging navigation, information hierarchy, legibility, and whether each diagram earns its space, I find that the main guide (Sections 01–07) establishes a clear high-level narrative for why a Cardano application attaches proofs to transactions, how the 35 CASH partial invoice arithmetic separates the 2 CASH program fee from debt reduction, why Groth16 requires 1 shared Phase 1 + N circuit-specific Phase 2 setups, and how the 4-step issuance route separates proof verification (Issue transactions) from state transition (Settlement transaction). However, the visual diagrams and mobile interaction design do not earn their space, and critical technical mechanics are either missing or buried in unreadable internal audit shorthand in Section 08. Specifically: (1) On mobile ('mobile-invoice-diagram.png'), the Section 02 Application Explorer stacks the 'Selected check' inspector ~350px below the 3 condition buttons, caption, and coverage callout, so tapping a condition updates text out of view and toggling 'Remove proof coverage' at the bottom mutates the diagram above the fold; (2) All 5 application diagrams ('invoice', 'dex', 'issuance', 'loan', 'treasury') reuse the exact same static 3-boxes-to-1-circle hub with zero numbers, zero UTxO inputs/outputs, and a visual structure that obscures how 1 whole-execution proof maps to 3 conditions, Strands, and on-chain claim outputs; (3) Section 03 ('settlement-stages.png') is just 4 columns of prose with no UTxO/transaction diagram showing the n-Issue-to-1-Settlement fan-in, signer roles, or post-expiry reclaim path; (4) The hero artwork ('desktop-opening.png') is purely decorative and the setup counter ('setup-counter.png') is a trivial '1 + N' stepper; (5) Directional and navigation cues are broken ('Change the amount ↓' in Section 02 points downward to Section 01 above it, '↗' is used for local tabs, internal anchors, and external links alike, and Sections 04/06/07 are missing from the top nav); and (6) Section 08 dumps undefined internal ticket/test codes ('T1/T2/T3', 'WP', 'N5/N7–N9 at V', 'ERR-xx / CL-xx') before the glossary appears.
